title: Hypocalcaemia (adult)
subject: nephrology
summary: Treat severe or symptomatic hypocalcaemia with 10 to 20 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV over 10 minutes then a calcium gluconate infusion, correct magnesium, and treat the cause with oral calcium, active vitamin D or vitamin D repletion.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Use albumin-adjusted calcium: adjusted calcium (mmol/L) = measured + 0.02 x (40 minus albumin in g/L). Check ionised calcium in critical illness or with very abnormal albumin.
Severe: adjusted calcium below 1.9 mmol/L (7.6 mg/dL) and/or symptoms at any level below the reference range. Mild: asymptomatic and above 1.9 mmol/L.
Features: perioral and digital paraesthesia, cramps, carpopedal spasm, Trousseau and Chvostek signs, laryngospasm, bronchospasm, seizures, prolonged QT, arrhythmia, hypotension.

Causes: post-thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy (commonest acute cause in hospital), vitamin D deficiency, hypomagnesaemia (including PPI-related), CKD, pancreatitis, rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, massive transfusion, bisphosphonates or denosumab, and respiratory alkalosis lowering ionised calcium.

sections.title: Severe or symptomatic: IV calcium
items: This is an emergency. Give 10 to 20 mL of 10% calcium gluconate in 50 to 100 mL of 5% dextrose IV over 10 minutes with ECG monitoring. Repeat until symptoms resolve.

Then start an infusion: 100 mL of 10% calcium gluconate (10 ampoules) in 1 L of 0.9% saline or 5% dextrose at 50 to 100 mL/h, titrated to keep calcium at the low end of normal until the cause is treated.
10 mL/kg of this infusion over 4 to 6 hours is expected to raise serum calcium by about 0.3 to 0.5 mmol/L.
Calcium chloride is more irritant and should be given only via a central line. 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate (2.2 mmol) equals 4.4 mL of 7.35% or 2.2 mL of 14.7% calcium chloride.
Use a large vein; do not mix calcium with sodium bicarbonate or phosphate. Continuous ECG monitoring for patients on digoxin or with arrhythmia.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Adjusted calcium, phosphate, magnesium, PTH, 25-hydroxy vitamin D, creatinine and electrolytes, ALP, and ECG for QT interval.
Send PTH and vitamin D before treatment where possible: low or inappropriately normal PTH suggests hypoparathyroidism or hypomagnesaemia; high PTH suggests vitamin D deficiency, CKD or resistance.
Check amylase or lipase, CK and urate when pancreatitis, rhabdomyolysis or tumour lysis is possible.

sections.title: Correct magnesium and treat the cause
items: Correct low magnesium first, or calcium will not stay up: stop the culprit drug and give magnesium sulphate 24 mmol (6 g) IV in 500 mL 0.9% saline or 5% dextrose over 24 hours, then recheck.
Mild hypocalcaemia: oral elemental calcium about 1 to 2 g daily in divided doses (for example calcium carbonate 500 mg elemental calcium tablets), with weekly calcium checks.
Hypoparathyroidism (including post-operative): alfacalcidol or calcitriol 0.25 to 0.5 mcg daily to start, with frequent calcium checks because active vitamin D can cause hypercalcaemia.
Vitamin D deficiency: load with about 300,000 units of cholecalciferol over 6 to 10 weeks (in India, 60,000-unit sachets make this 5 doses), with oral calcium.
Correct high phosphate where present; in advanced CKD or dialysis avoid large-volume calcium infusions and seek renal advice.

sections.title: After thyroid or parathyroid surgery
items: Post-thyroidectomy and asymptomatic: start oral calcium (SfE regimens use about 4 g elemental calcium daily in divided doses) and repeat calcium at 24 hours.
Adjusted calcium above 2.1 mmol/L (8.4 mg/dL): may be discharged with a calcium check within 1 week. Between 1.9 and 2.1 mmol/L: increase oral calcium.
Still mildly low beyond 72 hours despite oral calcium: add alfacalcidol 0.25 mcg daily with close monitoring.

After parathyroidectomy for severe hyperparathyroidism, hungry bone syndrome can cause profound, prolonged hypocalcaemia with low phosphate and magnesium: needs IV calcium, active vitamin D and specialist care.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: During IV infusion: adjusted calcium every 4 to 6 hours and 1 to 2 hours after a bolus; ECG monitoring.
Watch the infusion site for phlebitis and extravasation, which causes tissue necrosis.
On alfacalcidol or calcitriol: check calcium about 1 week after discharge, then at 1, 3 and 6 months; specialist follow-up.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating calcium without checking magnesium.
Treating low total calcium due only to low albumin.
Correcting calcium early in rhabdomyolysis or tumour lysis without symptoms, which promotes calcium phosphate deposition.
Rapid IV calcium in patients on digoxin without monitoring.

drugs.name: Calcium gluconate 10% (bolus)
drugs.dose: 10 to 20 mL in 50 to 100 mL 5% dextrose IV over 10 minutes, repeat until asymptomatic
drugs.notes: 10 mL contains 2.2 mmol calcium. ECG monitoring.

drugs.name: Calcium gluconate 10% (infusion)
drugs.dose: 100 mL in 1 L 0.9% saline or 5% dextrose at 50 to 100 mL/h, titrated to calcium
drugs.notes: Continue until the cause is treated; recheck calcium every 4 to 6 hours.

drugs.name: Magnesium sulphate
drugs.dose: 24 mmol (6 g) IV in 500 mL over 24 hours

drugs.name: Alfacalcidol or calcitriol
drugs.dose: 0.25 to 0.5 mcg orally daily to start
drugs.notes: Hypoparathyroidism; risk of hypercalcaemia, monitor closely.

drugs.name: Oral calcium (elemental)
drugs.dose: About 1 to 2 g daily in divided doses for mild hypocalcaemia

drugs.name: Cholecalciferol
drugs.dose: Total about 300,000 units over 6 to 10 weeks
drugs.notes: Vitamin D deficiency; give with calcium.
